questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish remote process invocation from a data-synchronization pattern like Bulk API sync?
options: Remote process invocation only ever happens asynchronously, while data sync is always synchronous
There is no real distinction; the two terms describe the same thing
Remote process invocation triggers a unit of work on another system where the outcome matters, rather than simply moving a data value from one place to another
Remote process invocation can only be used with the SOAP API
questions.explain: Remote process invocation is about triggering an action on another system and caring about its outcome — a tax calculation, a fraud check, a document generation — distinct from simply moving a data value between systems.

questions.q: What does RPC-style invocation optimize for, and what does it cost in exchange?
options: It optimizes for simplicity — making a remote call feel like calling a local function — at the cost of exposing the caller to the remote system's latency and failure modes as its own
It optimizes for guaranteed delivery and costs nothing in exchange
It optimizes for decoupling and has no latency cost at all
It optimizes for large data volume and is unrelated to latency
questions.explain: RPC-style invocation's appeal is making a remote call feel local and simple for the developer, but that comes at the cost of the same availability coupling from Lesson 6 — the caller is exposed to the remote system's latency and failures directly.

questions.q: How does request-reply messaging differ from RPC-style invocation in how it handles the call and its response?
options: It eliminates the need for any correlation between a request and its reply
It is only usable when no response is ever needed at all
It requires the remote system to always respond within one second

It decouples the request and reply using correlated messages rather than a direct, blocking call, so the caller isn't blocked waiting and a temporarily unavailable remote system doesn't immediately break the caller
questions.explain: Request-reply messaging trades RPC's simplicity for resilience by decoupling the call: the request is published as a message, processed on the remote system's own schedule, and the reply correlates back using the same correlation-ID idea from Lesson 7.

questions.q: Which Salesforce mechanism lets a remote process invocation run asynchronously relative to the transaction that triggered it, without blocking the user's save?
options: A synchronous Apex HTTP callout within the same transaction
Queueable Apex
A hard-coded callout with no Named Credential
The Metadata API
questions.explain: Queueable Apex lets a process be enqueued and run asynchronously relative to the transaction that triggered it — useful when the remote invocation doesn't need to block the user's save and can be processed moments later instead.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say failure handling is especially important for remote process invocation, more so than for a simple data sync?
options: Because remote process invocation never fails in practice
Because remote process invocation is always synchronous and therefore immune to ambiguity

Because a failure partway through can leave the two systems disagreeing about what actually happened — one thinks the call failed, the other thinks it succeeded — raising the question of whether a retry is safe
Because failure handling is actually unnecessary for invocation patterns and only matters for data sync
questions.explain: Because invocation triggers an action rather than moving a value, an ambiguous failure (a timeout after the remote system may have already started or finished its work) can leave the two systems disagreeing about the true outcome — exactly the problem idempotency, covered in Lesson 15, exists to address.
